## Methods

Materials
All reagents and catalysts used in this study were purchased from commercial suppliers and used without further purification unless stated otherwise. 2,2’-bipyridine, 1,5-cyclooctadiene (COD), and bis(1,5-cyclooctadiene)nickel (0) [Ni(COD)2] were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. All other drugs used in the synthesis process were obtained from Adamas-beta. Dimethylformamide (DMF) was dried over calcium hydride (CaH2) and then distilled under a dry nitrogen atmosphere immediately before use. Toluene was dried over sodium (Na) and subsequently distilled under a dry nitrogen atmosphere immediately before use. Anhydrous THF (HPLC grade) was obtained from Solvent Purification Systems (Innovative Technology, Inc.). PEDOT:PSS (Clevios PV P AI 4083) was purchased from Heraeus. The detailed synthesis of PDODPF was provided in the Supplementary Information. The PEODPF, PODPF, and POYDPF used in this paper was synthesized by our previous work.

Preparation of polymer solution, the pristine film (film) and the spherulite film (spherulite)
Polymer solution. The polymer solutions were prepared by dissolving the PEODPF polymer in the chloroform (CF) solvent spontaneously overnight. Various concentrated polymers solution for the spin-coating process is obtained after the heated solution cools to room temperature.

Spin-coated films (Film). Pristine films were spin-casted on quartz or silicon substrates from CF solution (various concentrations) using KW-4A (from the Institute of Micro-electronics of the Chinese Academy of Science) at 1500 for 60 s.

Spherulite films (Spherulite). The spherulite films were prepared by the solvent vapor annealing (SVA) method in Supplementary Fig. 5b. The spin-coated or drop-coated film was placed in a weighing bottle containing chloroform solvent, then the airtight weighing bottle into the oven, setting the oven temperature, and waiting for the chloroform solvent to finish evaporating to get the spherulite film.

Fabrication of polymer light-emitting diodes (PLEDs)
The PLEDs structure is ITO/PEDOT: PSS (50 nm)/EML/TPBi (23 nm)/LiF (1 nm)/Al (100 nm). The detailed fabrication procedure of PLEDs was described as follows. Before spin-coating, the ITO substrate was cleaned in an ultrasonic bath with detergent, acetone, isopropanol and deionized water, dried in an oven at 120 °C for 2 h, and treated with ultraviolet ozone for 10 min. In the spin-coating procedure, a 40 nm thick PEDOT:PSS was firstly spin-coated (Supplementary Fig. 15a, Step 1) and annealed at 120 °C for 20 min (Supplementary Fig. 15a, Step 2). Then, the emitting layer was spin-coated from CF solution (6 mg mL−1) (Supplementary Fig. 15a, Step 3) and the spherulite films were prepared by the SVA method (Supplementary Fig. 15a, Step 4). Next, Film and Spherulite film annealed at 100 °C for 10 min in a nitrogen-filled glovebox. Finally, the other layers, such as 23 nm TPBi, 1 nm LiF and 100 nm Al, were deposited by thermal evaporating sequentially through a shadow mask at a pressure below 1 × 10−5 mbar. The area of the device was 4 mm2 defined by the overlap between the ITO and Al electrode. The EL spectra were measured using a QE65 Pro (Ocean Optics) spectrometer in air with encapsulated devices. The structure of single carrier devices ITO/PEDOT: PSS/EML/MoO3/Al single carrier devices (hole-only) and ITO/ZnO/EML/TPBi/LiF/Al (electron-only) were prepared.

Characterization
General characterization. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were recorded using a JEOL NMR spectrometer (JNMECZ400S, 400 MHz, Japan), 1H NMR and 13C NMR spectra were referenced to CDCl3 (1H NMR: 7.26 ppm, 13C NMR: 77.0 ppm). Absorption spectra were measured with a Shimadzu UV-3600 spectrometer at room temperature, and emission spectra were recorded on a Hitachi F-4600 luminescence spectrometer. Nanosecond time-resolved studies were performed with an Edinburgh FLS980 time-correlated single photon-counting (TCSPC). The transient signal was acquired by TCSPC. Raman microscopy was performed using a Renishaw 2000 CCD spectrometer coupled to an Olympus BH-2 confocal microscope, and using the 633 nm line of a He–Ne laser as the excitation source to avoid absorption and resonance effects. The excitation energy-dependent PLQY of spherulite and pristine film samples were determined by a self-made system by combining a laser (MDL-III-375 nm, spot size is ≈0.13 cm2), an optical fiber, a spectrometer, and an integrating sphere. All films were deposited onto quartz substrates through spin-coating.

Grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) test. The GIWAXS measurement was performed at the BL14B1 beamline of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF) using an X-ray with a wavelength of 1.24 Å. The X-ray beam size was ≈0.2 mm × 0.3 mm, as defined by the horizontal and vertical slits.

Film morphology characterization. The polarized optical microscopy (POM) images were performed by NIKON LV100ND. AFM measurement was performed on Park XE-70 atomic force microscopy. Using tapping mode with as little force as possible to collect the topography and phase image of the sample at the same time, the scanning rate was 1 Hz, and the scanning range was 500 nm to 5 μm to obtain the results. The samples were then examined with a field emission SEM (Hitachi, S-4800) at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. The transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations were performed with an FEI Talos F200X microscope operated at 200 kV. (Point resolution 0.25 nm)

Femtosecond-transient absorption (fs-TA) test. Ultrafast TA spectroscopy was conducted using a Ti:sapphire regenerative amplifier (Libra, Coherent Inc.). The second harmonic of the primary beam at 400 nm or an optical parametric amplifier (OperA Solo, Coherent Inc.) pumped by the regenerative amplifier was used to generate the pump beam. The probe beam was a broadband supercontinuum light source generated by focusing a small portion of the femtosecond laser beam onto either a 5-mm-thick CaF2 plate. The TA signal was then analyzed by a silicon charge-coupled device mounted on a monochromater (Acton 2358, Princeton Instrument) at 1 kHz, enabled by a home-built control board.

Transient photoluminescence microscopies (TPLM) test. Photoexcitation diffusion imaging was performed using a home-built TPLM (Supplementary Fig. 12), a 405 nm picosecond pulsed laser (ALPHA-LAS) with a repetition rate of 10 MHz and pulse width of 25 ps was focused onto the surface of the sample using an objective lens (Olympus, 100X, Apo, 0.95 numerical aperture). Additionally, the single-photon detecting avalanche photodiode (APD) (SPCM-AQRH, dead time of 28 ns) was used to detect the PL, and the APD was connected to timing electronics (PicoQuant PicoHarp 3000). The measurement of time-resolved PL decay was based on the same excitation light path of the home-built TPLM, but the PL signal was collected by leading it out of the TPLM system through a multimode fiber (Thorlabs, ø50 μm, 5 m) with a pair of couplers and collimators (Thorlabs RC08FC-P01) and sending it to another APD (MPD PDM Series 20 μm) that was also attached to the timing electronics (PicoQuant PicoHarp 300), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 13.

Photothermal deflection spectroscopy (PDS) test. The measurement of PDS was based on NANOUPE-PDS-1. The testing scanning range of 350–600 nm. The absorption detection limit of PDS was 0.001%. The thermal deflection solution was 3 M Flourinert.

Transient electroluminescence (Tr-EL) measurement. The Agilent pulse generator (8114A, 100 V/2 A, rise time < 7 ns) is used to provide rectangular pulse voltages (repetition rate: 1 kHz or 100 Hz, pulse width: 3 or 5 μs) to drive the PLED. Emissions are collected by a Hamamatsu PTM (H10721–20, rise time: 0.57 ns), which is connected to a digital oscilloscope (Agilent DSOX4024A, bandwidth: 200 MHz).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors present a study on long-range exciton transport in π-conjugated polymer (πCP) films treated by solvent thermal annealing (SVA), and investigates their potential for improving exciton diffusion lengths. The authors show significant advancements, including submillimeter-scale spherulite formation, longer exciton diffusion lengths, and enhanced electroluminescence in PLEDs. While the study has a wide range of characterisation methods covered, I regret that I cannot recommend this manuscript for publication in its current form due to the following major concerns:
1. The authors used photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) values in their calculations; however, these values are not explicitly reported in the manuscript or supporting information. The measured PLQY values are essential for the comparison between the spherulite and pristine film samples and to access the reliability of the calculation.
2. The transient absorption (TA) measurements were measured at an intensity of up to 10 mOD, which is very high for systems with good diffusion lengths, especially in films. Under these conditions, exciton annihilation is very likely happening, making the kinetics faster and the comparison invalid. The authors should perform a fluence-dependent TA series in both the pristine and spherulite films to identify a low-fluence regime where no annihilation occurs. In this regime, the lifetimes should be compared.
3. Regarding the response time of the experimental setup, the authors should clarify whether the 0-300 ns range, where the diffusion constant is extracted, is within the response time of the system. If so, this time point may not be representative and needs careful consideration.
4. The authors extracted diffusion data for the first 300 ps despite the reported lifetime of 1.2 ns. However, Figure S7 reveals a negative trend after 300 ps, which is not adequately explained. The authors should provide a clear justification for excluding this part of the data although it is within the life time and address why the trend goes negative.
5. The Gaussian fits used in the analysis should be included in the Supplementary Information to allow readers to evaluate the robustness of the fitting procedure.
6. While the manuscript focuses on singlet exciton dynamics, it does not address the potential influence of triplet excitons in the devices. Optical excitation generates 100% singlet excitons, whilst triplet excitons only form via intersystem crossing (ISC). In contrast, electrical excitation directly produces 75% triplet excitons. The rising electroluminescence (EL) intensity trend observed in the spherulite films could be influenced by delayed triplet excitons contributing through triplet-triplet annihilation, especially given the efficient diffusion reported. The authors should discuss the role of triplet excitons in detail.
7. The authors should compare the PLQY and EQE values, as such a comparison can offer insights into the presence of trap states or dark triplet excitons, which could influence the overall device performance.

### Reviewer 2

This paper presents an innovative method to improve exciton transport in organic semiconductor materials. It involves creating submillimeter-scale spherulite films through solvent vapor annealing (SVA). The authors report substantial enhancements in exciton diffusion length and coefficients within π-conjugated polymer films, which show great promise for optoelectronic applications, especially in polymer light-emitting diodes (PLEDs). The study is well-structured, featuring comprehensive experimental methods, and the results offer valuable insights into how long-range ordered spherulite structures can significantly improve exciton diffusion and optoelectronic properties. This research deepens our understanding of the structural dynamics and performance of organic semiconductor materials. Therefore, this work can be considered for publication after a minor revision by addressing the following comments.
1. The paper suggests that the introduction of branched side chains, as opposed to linear side chains, leads to the formation of large-sized spherulites. Why does the introduction of branched side chains result in the formation of spherulites, while materials with linear side chains do not form this morphology? A comparative experiment should be conducted to explore this issue.
2. The description of “solvent vapor annealing” in the paper should be standardized, as there are currently two different expressions being used, such as “solvent thermal annealing”.
3. In Fig. 3b, why is the absorption edge of the spherulite higher than that of the pristine film?
4. Page 8, line 27; “We obtained the width of the bandgap tail states (Eu) by fitting the photothermal deflection spectroscopy (PDS). The Eu value of spherulite film is 48.1 meV, lower than the 52.9 meV of pristine spin-coated film (Fig. 3e).” In the PDS test referenced in the paper, the data obtained indicates minimal differences. Might these data potentially contain errors?
5. Page 10, line 13; “As shown in Fig. 4a, the diameter of excitation spot (beam center) irradiated on the nanofiber bundles is about 238 nm, covering several single nanofibers. ” This paper utilizes a laser with an excitation wavelength of 405 nm to excite the sample. How is the diameter of the light spot determined to be 238 nm? In Fig. S6, what is the role of the flip mirror?

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript studies exciton transport in a conjugated polymer by transient photoluminescence microscopy. Diffusion coefficients reach in the same order of magnitude as those of other reports in literature. Based on a solvent vapour annealing procedure of a spin coated film of branched side-chain modified polydiarylfluorene, the authors demonstrate improved structural order and ehanced exciton diffusivity. When incorporated into polymer light-emitting diodes, these films yield deep-blue electroluminescence with high brightness and improved color purity at low current densities.
Although the manuscript provides a detailed analysis of the structural and photophysical properties of the spherulite films, the core findings are not strikingly novel. The enhancement of exciton diffusion through improved molecular ordering and reduced defects in π-conjugated polymer films is a concept that is established in the literature. While the work confirms these relationships for the specific polymer under study, it does not introduce fundamentally novel insights or processing strategies. I am not sure about the impact of this work. In summary, the study confirms established principles rather than presenting research of great novelty that I would expect for papers in Nature Communications.
